component-sandwich-attack-intro-1: Before a transaction is included in a block, it usually waits in the public <glossary>mempool</glossary>, the shared waiting room for pending transactions. Anyone can read it there.
component-sandwich-attack-intro-2: A sandwich bot watches for swaps big enough to move a price. The bot pays the <glossary>block builder</glossary>, the service that puts the block together, to place its trades around yours: one just before and one just after. You get a worse price, and the bot keeps the difference.
component-sandwich-attack-intro-3: Try sending the same swap two ways.
component-sandwich-attack-slippage-help: <glossary>Slippage</glossary> is how far the price can move against you before your swap is cancelled instead of going through.
component-sandwich-attack-panel-mempool-: Each line is a pending transaction and the tip it offers, in <glossary>gwei</glossary> (a billionth of an ETH).
component-sandwich-attack-log-mint: mint {count, plural, one {# NFT} other {# NFTs}}
component-sandwich-attack-log-tag-you-pu: you, readable in the mempool for {duration}
component-sandwich-attack-log-mempool-bu: The bot's trades never appear here. It sends them, with a copy of your swap, straight to a block builder.
component-sandwich-attack-log-mempool-pr: Nothing new here: your swap isn't in the public mempool.
component-sandwich-attack-verdict-idle-p: Press Swap to send it the way many wallets do by default.
Press Swap to send it straight to a block builder.
component-sandwich-attack-verdict-waitin: Your swap is waiting in the public mempool, where anyone can read it.
component-sandwich-attack-verdict-bundle: The bot sends the builder a bundle: its sell, then your swap, then its buy-back. It pays the builder to keep that order.
component-sandwich-attack-verdict-result: The bot took {lost} because it could read your trade before it was included.
component-sandwich-attack-verdict-privat: Your swap goes straight to a block builder. It never enters the public mempool.
component-sandwich-attack-verdict-result: No sandwich: the bots never saw it. The private channel did, and you trusted it to pass your trade on.
component-sandwich-attack-private-caveat: A private transaction channel, sometimes called an MEV-protected RPC, moves the trust rather than removing it. The channel sees your transaction and, unless you connect through Tor or a similar network, your IP address.

Some channels also share hints about your pending transaction with searchers, the bots that look for <glossary>MEV</glossary>, usually in return for paying you back part of the value. What a channel shares, and with whom, is worth checking before you rely on it.
component-sandwich-attack-tech-summary: The technical bit: why the order of transactions matters
component-sandwich-attack-tech-1: Most token swaps trade against a pool that sets its price from its own balances, so every trade moves that price. The bot sells first, so the price you get is lower. Your trade pushes it lower still. Then the bot buys back cheaper than it sold.
component-sandwich-attack-tech-2: The bot doesn't need to outbid anyone in the public mempool. It sends its two trades and your swap to a block builder as one bundle, and pays the builder to place its trades around yours.
component-sandwich-attack-tech-3: Your slippage setting caps how much a bot can take. Set it too tight and your swap may fail instead.
component-sandwich-attack-caption: Amounts are illustrative. The order of events is how a sandwich works.
